about: Real Boltz-2 folds recorded on qb2. Every frame is a sampler state; see README.md.

entries.name: Insulin
entries.story: The hormone in every insulin pen: two short chains held together by sulfur bridges.
entries.why: Everyone knows someone who injects it. The smallest pick, so its surface is a pebble next to the rest.

entries.name: Green fluorescent protein
entries.story: A jellyfish protein that glows green. Biologists put it in cells to watch them live.
entries.why: A barrel with its light inside, a shape anyone can read; the S65T variant every lab uses, 2008 Nobel Prize.

entries.name: Haemoglobin
entries.story: Carries the oxygen you are breathing right now. Four chains, each holding an iron in a heme.
entries.why: The protein in every visitor's blood; four chains and four hemes make a big, symmetric surface.

entries.name: Myoglobin
entries.story: The first protein anyone saw in 3D, in 1958. It stores oxygen in whale muscle for the long dive.
entries.why: A history moment for a room of scientists, and the one-chain cousin of haemoglobin, so the two read as a pair.

entries.name: The coronavirus spike meets ACE2
entries.story: How the coronavirus gets in: the tip of its spike grabbing a receptor on a human cell.
entries.why: The pandemic everyone lived through, and the largest pick at over 800 residues.

entries.name: An antibody finds its target
entries.story: An antibody drug, etesevimab, grabbing the same spike tip so the virus cannot use it.
entries.why: The Y-shaped molecule everyone has heard of, caught in the act: the two antibody chains and their target.

entries.name: A designed binder
entries.story: A protein invented on a computer, not by evolution, that blocks the spike where ACE2 would hold it.
entries.why: LCB1 (Cao et al., 2020) shows what protein design does now, which is why a design platform exists.

entries.name: PETase
entries.story: An enzyme from a bacterium found at a bottle-recycling plant. It eats PET plastic.
entries.why: The plastics story a non-biologist repeats to friends, in a compact enzyme.

entries.name: Lysozyme
entries.story: In your tears and saliva. It cuts the walls of bacteria open.
entries.why: A protein in your own body doing a job you can feel. Small and round, its surface reads as one smooth stone.

entries.name: Top7
entries.story: The first protein shape invented by a computer, in 2003. Nature never made it.
entries.why: Protein design started here (Kuhlman et al., 2003). It pairs with the designed binder for the design story.

entries.name: A T cell checks for a virus
entries.story: How your immune system spots an infected cell: a T cell receptor reading a scrap of virus that the cell holds up in HLA.
entries.why: Five chains and the core of how T cells, vaccines and cell therapies work: HLA-A2 holding the HTLV-1 Tax peptide, read by the A6 receptor (Garboczi et al., 1996).

entries.name: Keytruda blocks PD-1
entries.story: The best-selling cancer drug: an antibody that covers PD-1 so tumours cannot switch off the T cells attacking them.
entries.why: Pembrolizumab, the immunotherapy most visitors have heard of, as its Fab bound to human PD-1.

entries.name: Paxlovid jams the coronavirus
entries.story: The COVID pill at work: nirmatrelvir sitting in both halves of the enzyme the virus needs to copy itself.
entries.why: A drug designed in months during the pandemic, in its target: the main protease dimer with one nirmatrelvir in each active site.
